from_notes: - APPSC G1 2024 statements: "suspensive veto in Money Bills but not Finance Bills" – **false** (the reverse); "absolute veto on Government Bills at all times" – **false**; "**pocket veto indefinitely; the American President has a qualified veto**" – **true**; "objective = checks and balances between the President's office and Parliament" – **false** (the stated objects are to **prevent hasty, ill-considered or unconstitutional legislation**) → **only III**. | Pocket | Neither assents, rejects nor returns – keeps the Bill pending indefinitely | Possible because Art. 111 prescribes no time limit
x: Only III is valid: the President holds the pocket veto without time limit while the US President has a qualified veto. I reverses the rule (no suspensive veto on Money Bills), II is wrong (absolute veto on Government Bills only when the Cabinet resigns), and IV is not the object – the veto exists to prevent hasty or unconstitutional legislation.
source: NextGen Polity - APPSC Exams (src/polity/nextgen-polity-full.txt) p.380-382; PMF Polity Notes Part 2 (src/polity/pmf-polity-02.txt) p.2; Laxmikanth, Indian Polity ch. President

x: Article 111 lets the President assent, withhold assent or return a non-Money Bill passed by both Houses; Art. 108 is the joint sitting, Art. 109 Money Bill procedure and Art. 63 the Vice-President.

from_notes: Pocket | Neither assents, rejects nor returns – keeps the Bill pending indefinitely | Possible because Art. 111 prescribes no time limit
